prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a simple but important mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful proof trajectories, yet at inference time they operate inside a search process that repeatedly proposes tactics, observes failures, and backtracks. The authors propose to train on trial-and-error traces that include failed branches and backtracking, and they instantiate this idea on a newly curated Lean dataset for intuitionistic propositional logic, PropL. Empirically, they report that their model, TrialMaster, achieves substantially better out-of-distribution proving performance than a conventional model trained only on successful proofs, while also reducing search cost measured by Lean calls. The central idea is intuitive and worthwhile, and the paper’s strongest contribution is to make this training/inference mismatch explicit and test it in a controlled formal setting.

I found the paper interesting and potentially valuable, especially because it isolates a concrete hypothesis in a domain where correctness can be mechanically checked. The use of intuitionistic propositional logic is a reasonable first testbed: it is expressive enough to require nontrivial proof search and backtracking, but constrained enough that one can generate large amounts of verified data and analyze behavior carefully. The reported gap in OOD success rate between TrialMaster and the ablated model trained without trial-and-error information is large, and if robust, would be a meaningful result. The dataset contribution also seems useful, particularly if the released traces indeed contain complete search histories rather than only successful paths.

That said, I have substantial concerns about the experimental design, the fairness of the main comparison, and the strength of the claims. In its current form, the paper provides promising evidence for the usefulness of failure-aware training, but it does not yet convincingly establish that the gains come specifically from learning from failed attempts rather than from differences in inference protocol, supervision format, or search budget.

The main issue is that the comparison between TrialMaster and the DFS baseline is not clean. TrialMaster is trained on trial-and-error traces and then run in a bespoke autoregressive interaction loop where it sees the entire proof history, can emit explicit backtrack instructions, and uses greedy decoding of one action at a time. The DFS baseline is trained on successful proofs only and then used as a tactic sampler inside an external DFS procedure with temperature and multiple sampled tactics per state. These are not matched inference settings. The paper partly addresses this with the ablation “Model - proof w/o t.a.e.”, which uses the same inference style as TrialMaster but is trained without trial-and-error data. This ablation is actually the most convincing experiment in the paper, because it better isolates the effect of the training data. In contrast, the headline comparison against DFS conflates at least three factors: training data, action space, and search controller. I would strongly encourage the authors to elevate the matched-inference ablation to the primary result and de-emphasize the DFS comparison unless they can make it more controlled.

Relatedly, TrialMaster’s action space includes a special backtrack instruction, whereas the baseline model appears only to emit Lean tactics and relies on an external DFS controller for backtracking. This is a meaningful architectural difference. If the model is explicitly trained to emit “no solution, return to state k,” then part of the gain may come from learning a compact search-control language rather than from negative examples per se. That is still interesting, but it is a different claim. A stronger experimental decomposition would compare: training with successful proofs only versus training with full traces, while holding fixed whether the model can emit backtrack tokens; and separately compare explicit backtrack-token supervision versus implicit failure-history conditioning.

A second concern is that the dataset generation process may bias the task toward the proposed method in ways that are not fully discussed. The proofs with trial-and-error are generated by a specific focused proof search algorithm with randomized choices during chaining. TrialMaster is then trained to imitate these traces, including their style of backtracking and state numbering. This raises the possibility that the model is learning the idiosyncrasies of one search procedure rather than a general principle of learning from failure. Since the same FPS-derived traces define both the training supervision and, indirectly, the notion of “useful” backtracking behavior, the setup is somewhat self-referential. It would help to know whether the gains persist when training traces are generated by one search policy and evaluation uses another, or when multiple trace-generation policies are mixed. Even a small experiment varying the trace generator would strengthen the claim that the model learns reusable failure-aware reasoning rather than overfitting to a trace format.

The paper repeatedly describes PropL as “complete, scalable, and representative,” and claims that uniform sampling over natural numbers via a bijection yields representative propositional formulas. This language is too strong as written. A bijection plus uniform sampling over a finite integer range gives a particular induced distribution over formulas of bounded size under the chosen encoding and ordering; it does not by itself establish representativeness for theorem proving difficulty, proof structure, or natural theorem distributions. Moreover, the train/test split is based on proof lengths under the authors’ proof-generation procedures, which further shapes the distribution. I think the dataset may well be useful and systematic, but the representativeness claim should be softened and made more precise.

There is also an important incompleteness caveat in the proof generator: the additional assumption that once an implication is picked, it cannot be used to show its premise introduces incompleteness, albeit reportedly affecting only about 1 in 1000 provable theorems. This is probably acceptable for dataset construction, but it matters for the interpretation of “complete proof trees” and “representative benchmark.” The paper should be clearer that the traces are complete with respect to the modified search procedure, not necessarily with respect to unrestricted proof search.

The evaluation metrics are sensible but somewhat asymmetric. Search cost is measured by the number of Lean calls, which favors TrialMaster because backtrack instructions are free under this metric. That is not unreasonable if Lean interaction is the dominant cost, but it should be acknowledged more explicitly that the metric ignores model-generation cost and prompt growth. TrialMaster repeatedly conditions on the entire proof tree and emits an entire continuation from which only the first tactic is used; this may be computationally expensive in token generation even if it saves Lean calls. Since one of the paper’s claims is efficiency, reporting wall-clock time, generated tokens, or average prompt length would provide a more balanced picture. As it stands, “lower search cost” really means “fewer theorem-checker invocations,” not necessarily lower end-to-end compute.

The stopping criteria are also not fully matched. TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, whereas the DFS system can continue exploring alternative sampled tactics at a state. This makes the 88.7% OOD success rate for TrialMaster more impressive, but it also means the systems have qualitatively different robustness profiles. More importantly, the 1500-word context limit is stricter for TrialMaster because its history includes failed branches and backtracking annotations. The authors mention this, which is good, but I would like to see statistics on how often each failure mode occurs for each method: Lean error, context overflow, search-step limit, exhausted tactics, etc. That would clarify whether TrialMaster’s gains come from better tactic quality, better backtracking decisions, or simply avoiding certain failure modes.

The empirical presentation is somewhat incomplete in the provided text. The paper refers to Figure 5 for the key OOD results and search-cost tradeoffs, but the exact numbers are not all visible here. Since the central claim rests on these comparisons, the paper should include a compact table with the best and representative configurations, confidence intervals or standard deviations across runs if applicable, and perhaps per-theorem success stratified by proof length. Given that decoding and sampling can introduce variance, especially for the DFS baseline, reporting results from multiple random seeds would be important.

I also think the paper could do more to analyze what the model actually learns from failure. The statement that all backtracking instructions are well-formed and point to existing states is encouraging but weak as evidence of meaningful backtracking competence. A stronger analysis would ask: when TrialMaster backtracks, how often does it backtrack to the same state that the FPS oracle would have chosen? How often does backtracking lead to eventual success versus repeated loops? Does the model avoid re-proposing previously failed tactics? Does conditioning on failed branches change the next-tactic distribution in measurable ways? The motivating Figure 1 suggests a distributional shift away from failed tactics, but the paper does not quantify this behavior.

The exploratory result that shorter trial-and-error proofs outperform longer ones is interesting, but the interpretation is underdeveloped. It may indicate that too much failure information is noisy, but it could also reflect context-length issues, optimization difficulty, or a mismatch between training trace verbosity and test-time decoding. This suggests a richer design space: selective inclusion of failures, weighting recent failures more heavily, compressing failed branches, or training with explicit contrastive objectives rather than raw trace imitation. The paper would benefit from discussing these possibilities, especially since the current method appears to rely on relatively short traces among the available candidates.

Another weakness is the limited baseline set. The paper compares primarily against a successful-proof-trained model in DFS and one matched-inference ablation. Given the related work discussion, it would be valuable to include at least one stronger failure-aware or history-aware baseline. For example, a model trained on successful proofs plus proof-assistant error messages, or a prompting baseline that includes failed attempts in context without fine-tuning, would help position the contribution. Even if such baselines are imperfect in this domain, they would clarify whether the gain comes from trial-and-error supervision specifically or simply from exposing the model to more history.

The classical logic claim is currently too under-supported. The introduction and results mention improved performance on classical logic problems when fine-tuned with a hybrid dataset, including a “10% increase in success rate,” but the paper excerpt provides almost no methodological detail or quantitative table for this setting. If classical logic generalization is meant to be a substantive claim, it needs its own experimental section with dataset construction, baseline details, and results. Otherwise, it should be framed as a preliminary observation rather than part of the main contribution.

On the positive side, the paper has several appealing aspects. The problem formulation is clear and motivated by a real mismatch in current theorem-proving pipelines. The use of Lean for verification gives the results credibility. The dataset generation pipeline is thoughtfully designed, and the attempt to create OOD splits by proof length is better than a random split. The matched-inference ablation in Table 3 is compelling and suggests that the core idea has merit. I also appreciate that the authors explicitly discuss limitations, including context length and the narrow domain.

There are also several presentation issues. The manuscript contains repeated sentences and duplicated claims, especially in the introduction and conclusion, which hurts readability and gives the impression of insufficient polishing. Some figures and tables appear malformed in the provided text. The notation around proof lengths and “word length” versus token length should be clarified. The paper should define exactly what is included in the model input and output format, ideally with one full prompt/completion example. It would also help to specify whether the 1500 limit is words, whitespace-separated tokens, or model tokenizer tokens, since this matters for reproducibility.

For improvement, my main recommendations are as follows. First, restructure the empirical section so that the primary comparison is between matched inference procedures, isolating the effect of trial-and-error training. Second, add stronger analyses of learned backtracking behavior and failure utilization. Third, report more complete statistics on failure modes, variance, and computational cost beyond Lean calls. Fourth, soften or better justify claims about representativeness and completeness of PropL. Fifth, either substantiate the classical logic extension properly or remove it from the main claims.

A few concrete experiments would significantly strengthen the paper. One would be a controlled comparison among four variants: successful-only training versus trial-and-error training, crossed with tactic-only outputs versus tactic-plus-backtrack outputs. Another would be to train on traces where failed branches are shuffled, truncated, or replaced with synthetic negatives, to test whether the exact sequential failure history matters. A third would be to compare against a baseline that simply appends previously failed tactics to the prompt at inference without special training. Finally, evaluating whether the learned policy transfers across different proof-search trace generators would address concerns about overfitting to FPS-specific trajectories.

Overall, I think the paper presents a promising idea and some encouraging evidence, but the current version overstates what has been established. The strongest takeaway supported by the experiments is that, in a controlled intuitionistic propositional logic setting, fine-tuning an LLM on proof traces that include failed attempts can substantially improve OOD proving performance under a matched autoregressive inference protocol. The broader claims about superior theorem proving, efficient search, and general significance beyond this setting need more careful qualification and stronger baselines. With a more rigorous experimental decomposition and tighter presentation, this could become a solid contribution. As it stands, I view it as borderline: interesting and potentially impactful, but not yet fully convincing by top-tier conference standards.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies whether large language models for theorem proving benefit from training on failed proof attempts in addition to successful proof paths. To enable this, the authors construct PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with proof trees generated by a focused proof search procedure, including backtracking information. They fine-tune Llama-2-7B in two settings: a conventional tactic generator trained only on successful proofs and used within DFS, and TrialMaster, trained on proofs with trial-and-error traces and allowed to emit both tactics and explicit backtrack instructions. On their PropL benchmark, TrialMaster reportedly achieves higher out-of-distribution success rate and lower Lean-call search cost than the DFS baseline, and an ablation suggests that removing trial-and-error data substantially hurts performance.
strengths: The paper addresses a real train-test mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful trajectories but used in search settings that repeatedly encounter failures.
The central idea is intuitive and potentially important: failed proof attempts may provide useful supervision for both tactic quality and backtracking behavior.
The authors build a new Lean-formalized dataset with proof-search traces, which is valuable because existing public datasets rarely expose failed branches explicitly.
The evaluation includes both success rate and a concrete search-cost metric based on Lean calls, which is appropriate for theorem proving systems.
The ablation comparing training with and without trial-and-error information supports the claim that the additional supervision is useful within their setup.
The paper is clearly motivated and the overall system design is easy to understand.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow: all main claims are established on synthetic intuitionistic propositional logic theorems generated by a deterministic proof-search procedure, which is far from realistic interactive theorem proving workloads.

The comparison is not fully apples-to-apples because TrialMaster and the DFS baseline differ in both training data and inference algorithm; improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to training on failures alone.

The paper repeatedly claims the dataset is 'complete, scalable, and representative,' but these claims are only weakly justified and may be overstated given the fixed theorem size, bounded atom count, and synthetic generation process.

Important experimental details are missing or unclear, including prompt formatting, exact tokenization/context accounting for the 1500-word limit, decoding details for TrialMaster, and variance across runs/seeds.
The reported gains on classical logic are mentioned but not properly described or substantiated in the provided results tables/figures.
The paper lacks comparisons to stronger or more relevant baselines from recent theorem-proving literature, including systems that use error feedback, repair, or search-aware prompting/fine-tuning.
The writing contains substantial repetition and some inconsistencies, which makes it harder to assess the exact contribution and experimental protocol.
methodological_flaws: The main causal claim—that training on failed trials improves theorem proving—is confounded by inference differences. TrialMaster emits explicit backtrack instructions and conditions on full search history, while the baseline uses DFS over sampled tactics. This means the observed gains cannot be attributed solely to the training signal from failures.

The dataset generation procedure introduces a known incompleteness in proof search ('once an implication is picked, the implication cannot be used to show its premise'). Although claimed to affect only about 1 in 1000 provable theorems, this weakens the claim that the dataset is complete and representative, and may bias the theorem/proof distribution.

The theorem split is based on proof lengths produced by the same deterministic/procedural generator used to create supervision. This may create a benchmark aligned with the generator’s own proof style rather than measuring broader generalization.

The claim of 'uniformly sampled from all possible theorems' is scientifically imprecise. A bijection from naturals to formulas plus uniform sampling over integers in a finite range does not imply a natural or unbiased distribution over semantically distinct theorems, provable theorems, or theorem difficulty; many syntactically different formulas may be trivial variants.

The success/failure criteria are asymmetric across methods. TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, while DFS can sample multiple tactics per state and continue exploring. Conversely, TrialMaster’s backtrack instructions incur no Lean cost. These design choices complicate direct efficiency comparisons.
No statistical uncertainty is reported despite evaluation on only 1000 OOD theorems. Differences such as 88.7% vs 88.4% may not be meaningful without confidence intervals or repeated runs.

The claim that the model 'learns backtracking capability' is weakly supported: producing syntactically valid references to prior states does not establish semantically effective backtracking beyond the aggregate success metric.
The paper does not provide rigorous evidence that the proposed method generalizes beyond the synthetic propositional setting; therefore broader conclusions about theorem proving are overstated.
